This is the first written piece of your team's proposal. It replaces
the one-page pitch announced in meetings 1 and 3.

## The assignment in brief

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **What** | A description of your project, up to three pages, and a three-minute talk about it |
| **Who** | One submission per team |
| **Weight** | 5 % of the course grade. Every member receives the same grade |
| **Due** | On [Canvas](https://canvas.cornell.edu/courses/92942/assignments/1030305) by 11:59 pm on Friday, October 23. Canvas asks for your NetID |
| **Length** | Up to three pages for the six sections. The references and the AI disclosure go on a separate page that does not count |
| **File** | One PDF, named `Team-A_project-description.pdf` with your team's letter |
| **Talk** | Three minutes in session B of meeting 10, on October 28, followed by one question from the room |
| **Examples** | Two worked examples by hypothetical teams. [Solar farms and home values](project-description-example-solar.qmd) asks a question a town would act on ([PDF](Team-X_project-description.pdf)). [Boycotts and store visits at Target](project-description-example-target.qmd) asks one a company would pay for ([PDF](Team-Y_project-description.pdf)) |

## What the document must contain

The first line of page 1 gives your team letter and a working title.
The second line lists every member's full name. A name on that line
means the member has read the document and agrees with it.

Then use the six headings below, numbered and worded as they are here,
in this order. Each one gives a rough length and the session-B sheet to
start from. If your team kept no copy of a sheet it handed in, ask me
for it.

### 1. Research question

About five to eight lines. Start from your meeting 3 [question
sheet](resource-map.qmd).

- State the question in one sentence ending with a question mark. It is
  the first sentence of the section.
- Name its shape from [meeting
  3](../sessions/03-questions.qmd#the-seven-shapes-in-full):
  evaluation, preference and pricing, prediction and risk, diagnosis,
  feasibility, measurement, or valuation.
- Name who would act on the answer or pay for it, by role. "The pricing
  manager of a regional grocery chain" is specific enough.
  "Policymakers" is too vague.
- State the answer you expect, with its direction and a rough size, and
  the result that would show you were wrong.

### 2. Why it matters

About half a page. Start from the line *Who acts on it, or pays for it*
and from filter 4 on your meeting 3 question sheet.

- Name the decision that would change with the answer, who makes it,
  and what they would do if the answer came out each way.
- Summarize your two or three [anchor
  papers](../sessions/05-tools-and-ai-slides.html#/what-an-anchor-paper-is),
  the published studies closest to yours, in one or two sentences each.
  Say what your project adds to them.
- Cite each study by author and year, and list it in the references.

### 3. Approach

About half a page, plus your causal graph if you include one. Start
from your [meeting 2](../sessions/02-causality.qmd#session-b-330430)
graph and from the lines you wrote at [meeting
8](../sessions/08-designs-i.qmd#session-b-330430) on whether an
experiment, an instrument or a discontinuity is open to you. A
photograph of your meeting 2 graph is fine if its labels are legible.

Every project states these three things.

- Name the unit of observation, such as a store-week or a household.
- Name the outcome, the variable that measures it, and its source.
- Describe the sample: which units, where, which years, and roughly how
  many. Say whether it covers the people or places that the decision in
  section 2 concerns.

If your question asks what a change caused, state these four as well.
A preference and pricing question belongs here, because the treatment
is the price or attribute you vary in your task.

- Name the **treatment**, the change whose effect you want to estimate.
- Describe the **comparison group** or period. Its outcomes stand in
  for the **counterfactual**, what the treated units would have done
  without the treatment.
- Name the research design, such as an experiment, instrumental
  variables, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences, or
  panel data with fixed effects.
- State the **identifying assumption** in one sentence. It is the
  assumption that makes your comparison a valid stand-in for the
  counterfactual.

If your question asks anything else, state this instead. That covers a
prediction, a measurement, a diagnosis, a feasibility study and a
valuation.

- Say what the answer has to get right to be useful, and how you will
  check it against something outside your own data. A prediction is
  checked by its error on data you held out. A measurement is checked
  against a count from another source. A valuation names its
  comparables and what makes them comparable. A diagnosis names the
  benchmark it measures the gap against. A feasibility study names the
  original data your team will analyze itself.

### 4. Data and access

About three quarters of a page. Start from your meeting 3 [resource
map](resource-map.qmd). I read this section first, because most
capstones that fail had a good question whose data never arrived.

Give one row per dataset, in a table with these six columns.

| Dataset | Holder | Unit and period | Variables you need | Access time | Status |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| *Example:* Weekly Patterns Plus | Dewey, through Cornell's subscription | Store-week, 2019–2024 | Weekly visits, store category, location | Days | File opened Oct 12 |

- **Access time** is your dataset's row on the [access
  ladder](../data-sources.qmd#the-access-ladder-read-this-one): now,
  days, weeks, months, or longer.
- **Status** is one of four entries: file opened, access requested, or
  holder contacted, each with its date, or not started.
- If you collect the data yourself, give the survey or experiment its
  own row. The holder is your team. The unit is the participant, and
  the period is when you will field it. The access time is weeks. The
  status is your stage, with its date: protocol submitted, instrument
  drafted, or not started.

Below the table, add three things.

- Give the date by which you expect to hold every dataset.
- Give your plan B, the question your project becomes if the data has
  not arrived by that date. If you already hold every dataset, give the
  question your project becomes if the data turns out not to contain
  what you need.
- Say whether the project needs an IRB application or a data-use
  agreement, or that you have asked the IRB office to decide, with the
  date you asked. Use your meeting 4 [IRB and DUA
  checklist](ethics-checklist.qmd). If the project needs an approval,
  give the date the slowest one has to start.

### 5. Anticipated challenges

About a third of a page. Start from the one-page threat your team wrote
at [meeting 7](../sessions/07-model-failures.qmd#session-b-330430).

Name two or three challenges. For each one, say what you will do if it
is not resolved, and by what date. One of them must be the main threat
to your estimate.

- For a causal question, name the source of bias in meeting 7's terms,
  such as selection into treatment or omitted variables. Say the
  direction in which it pushes the estimate, and whether you can
  measure the variable that would close it.
- For any other question, name the main way the answer could be wrong,
  and how you would find out.

The other challenges can be the row of your resource map most likely
to stop the project, or an approval you are still waiting for.

### 6. Team plan

About half a page, in two parts. Start from your meeting 2 [ground
rules](../teamwork.qmd#the-ground-rules-and-raci).

**Roles.** Give one row per member, in a table with these five
columns. Each *Delivers* cell names a specific output. Each *By* cell
gives a date before December 11, or a weekday for a task that repeats
every week. Name a coordinator, who runs the weekly check-in and
uploads the team's work. Name a backup for every main task. For
example:

| Member | Role | Delivers | By | Backup |
|:-----|:-------|:------------------------|:--------|:------|
| Farah | Coordinator | Runs the check-in. Uploads each deliverable | Every Wednesday | Gabe |
| Gabe | Data | Dewey account approved. First extract opened and described | Oct 30 | Hana |
| Hana | Design | Causal graph and identifying assumption, written for the outline | Nov 4 | Idris |
| Idris | Literature | Two more studies opened. What is already known, written for the outline | Nov 4 | Kofi |
| Kofi | Writing | Outline merged and edited into one voice | Nov 10 | Farah |

**Missed work.** Write the steps your team follows when a member does
not deliver. A miss is a task not done by its date without warning. A
member who warns the team before the date has not missed it, and the
team sets a new date at the next check-in. Give at least three numbered
steps, ending with the team bringing the problem to me. You may use
these three as written:

1. **First miss.** It is raised at the next check-in and written down,
   with a new date.
2. **Second miss.** The coordinator talks to the member that week. The
   task goes to the backup or is split, and the check-in records it.
3. **No change, or a week with no reply.** The team brings it to me,
   with the check-ins as the record.

## References and AI disclosure

These two items go on a separate page after the six sections. They do
not count toward the three pages, and nothing else goes on that page.

**References.** List every work you cite, in any consistent citation
style, each with a link or DOI. Your datasets belong in the section 4
table, so list one here only if you cite it in the text. Cite only
works you have opened. A citation to a work that does not exist is
treated as fabrication under the [AI policy](../syllabus.qmd#ai-policy).

**AI disclosure.** Write the three lines from [meeting
5](../sessions/05-tools-and-ai-slides.html#/what-you-write-down-about-what-you-used):
the tools you used, what you used them for, and what you checked. If
you used none, write "**Tools.** None." For example:

> **Tools.** Claude (claude.ai).\
> **Used for.** Finding candidate anchor papers. Tightening the wording
> of section 2.\
> **Checked.** We opened every reference and wrote each summary
> ourselves.

## Format and submission

- Use letter paper, one-inch margins, and 11-point type or larger.
  Single spacing is fine. Tables and figure labels may use 9-point
  type.
- Fit sections 1 to 6, including tables and figures, within three
  pages. I do not read anything past page 3 except the references and
  the AI disclosure. Do not add appendices.
- Name the file `Team-A_project-description.pdf`, with your team's
  letter.
- One member uploads it to the Canvas group assignment for the team. I
  do not accept submissions by email.
- You may resubmit before the deadline. I grade the last submission.
- The syllabus [late
  policy](../syllabus.qmd#what-you-are-graded-against) applies. A late
  submission loses 10 % up to 8 hours late and 50 % from 8 to 72 hours.
  After 72 hours it is not accepted.

## The talk at meeting 10

- Every team presents in session B of meeting 10, on Wednesday, October
  28. The order is drawn at random, so be ready from the start of
  session B.
- You have three minutes, timed, and I stop you at three. One question
  from the room follows.
- Cover the question, who acts on the answer, your approach, and your
  data with its status. For a causal question, the approach includes
  the design and its identifying assumption.
- Your team decides who speaks.
- Slides are optional, two at most. Attach them to the same Canvas
  submission as the description, as a second file named
  `Team-A_slides.pdf`. If you resubmit, attach both files again. I show
  the slides from the room computer.

## How it is graded

The document and the talk are scored together out of 100. That score is
worth 5 % of the course grade, and every member of the team receives
it.

| Part | Points |
|:--|--:|
| 1. Research question | 15 |
| 2. Why it matters | 10 |
| 3. Approach | 15 |
| 4. Data and access | 20 |
| 5. Anticipated challenges | 10 |
| 6. Team plan | 10 |
| The talk | 20 |
| **Total** | **100** |

Each part is scored on the [syllabus
scale](../syllabus.qmd#what-you-are-graded-against). Excellent earns
full points. Adequate earns three quarters and weak earns half. A part
that is missing, or so thin it shows no thought, earns zero. The talk
is scored on whether it covers the four items within three minutes, and
on how the team answers the question.

## Questions students ask

**Can we change our question after this?** Yes. Record the change and
the reason in your team's [decision
log](../teamwork.qmd#the-decision-log).

**We do not have the data yet. Is that a problem?** No. Show what you
have checked and requested, with dates, and give your plan B. A dataset
you have named but not checked scores weak.

**Our question does not ask what a change caused. Do we need a research
design?** No. Complete the last part of section 3 instead.

**We plan to use difference-in-differences, which meeting 9 covers two
days before the deadline. How much do we write?** Name the design,
describe the comparison in plain words, and state the identifying
assumption in one sentence, as the [solar
example](project-description-example-solar.qmd#approach) does: without
the treatment, the two groups would have followed the same trend.
[Remix](https://mixtape.scunning.com/) chapters 8 and 9 cover it, and
you refine it in the outline.

**Can the team lower a member's grade for not contributing?** No. Every
member receives the same grade on team work. Follow your missed-work
steps, which end with the team bringing the problem to me.

**Why do we have to write roles and a missed-work procedure?** Writing
them down early is standard practice, and there is evidence for it.
[Mathieu and Rapp](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0013257) followed 32 teams
of MBA students through a business strategy simulation. The teams that
sustained the best performance had written both a good team charter and
a good plan for the work. [Oakley and
colleagues](https://engr.ncsu.edu/wp-content/uploads/drive/1ofGhdOciEwloA2zofffqkr7jG3SeKRq3/2004-Oakley-paper%28JSCL%29.pdf)
give a template for both.
